```{r}
#| include: false
run_targets <- requireNamespace("targets", quietly = TRUE) &&
  requireNamespace("withr", quietly = TRUE)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  eval = run_targets,
  fig.width = 6,
  fig.height = 3.2,
  dpi = 120
)
# size each plot chunk from the plot itself (ggtargets::dag_size()), so
# nodes, lines and text look the same in every figure
knitr::opts_hooks$set(dag_fig = function(options) {
  code <- paste(options$code, collapse = "\n")
  if (!isTRUE(options$eval) || !grepl("ggplot_dag|tar_ggplot", code)) {
    return(options)
  }
  seed <- if (exists(".Random.seed", globalenv())) {
    get(".Random.seed", globalenv())
  }
  wd <- getwd()
  on.exit({
    setwd(wd)
    if (is.null(seed)) {
      suppressWarnings(rm(".Random.seed", envir = globalenv()))
    } else {
      assign(".Random.seed", seed, globalenv())
    }
  })
  root <- knitr::opts_knit$get("root.dir")
  if (!is.null(root)) {
    setwd(root)
  }
  size <- tryCatch(
    {
      p <- eval(parse(text = code), new.env(parent = knitr::knit_global()))
      if (ggplot2::is_ggplot(p) && !inherits(p, "patchwork")) {
        ggtargets::dag_size(p)
      }
    },
    error = function(e) NULL
  )
  if (!is.null(size)) {
    options$fig.width <- size[["width"]]
    options$fig.height <- size[["height"]]
  }
  options
})
knitr::opts_chunk$set(dag_fig = TRUE)
if (run_targets) {
  proj_dir <- tempfile("ggtargets-vignette-")
  dir.create(proj_dir)
  knitr::opts_knit$set(root.dir = proj_dir)
}
```

```{r}
#| label: setup
library(ggtargets)
library(targets)
```

ggtargets plots a [targets](https://docs.ropensci.org/targets/) pipeline as a ggplot2 object, in dagviz's "metro" style: one row per target, thick colored lines for dependencies, rounded bends where a lane changes column, and a white "bridge" wherever two lines cross.

## Write a small pipeline

`tar_script()` writes a `_targets.R` file. This one reads some numbers, cleans them, fits a model, and reports on it - `fit_model()` is a named function, not inlined, so the next section can edit just its body:

```{r}
#| label: pipeline
tar_script({
  fit_model <- function(data) stats::lm(y ~ x, data = data)

  list(
    tar_target(raw_data, data.frame(x = 1:20, y = 1:20 * 2 + stats::rnorm(20))),
    tar_target(clean_data, raw_data[stats::complete.cases(raw_data), ]),
    tar_target(model, fit_model(clean_data)),
    tar_target(
      summary,
      data.frame(
        term = names(stats::coef(model)),
        estimate = unname(stats::coef(model))
      )
    ),
    tar_target(
      report,
      paste(utils::capture.output(print(summary)), collapse = "\n")
    )
  )
})
```

## Plot it

`tar_ggplot()` is the one-call entry point: it reads the pipeline in the current directory and returns a plot.

```{r}
#| label: first-plot
#| fig-alt: "A metro-style plot of a five-target pipeline: raw_data, clean_data, model, summary, report, each in its own color, connected top to bottom."
tar_ggplot()
```

Reading the plot: each row is one target, in the pipeline's dependency order (a target's row always comes after everything it depends on). Each target gets its own color and lane; a lane runs straight down when nothing else needs the column, and curves left or right - a rounded bend, not a sharp corner - when it has to make room. The dotted gray line from each node to its label is just a leader line, not a dependency.

Before `tar_make()` runs, every target is `outdated` (targets doesn't distinguish "not yet built" from "needs a rebuild" - both are outdated). Color by status to see this directly:

```{r}
#| label: status-before
#| fig-alt: "The same pipeline, all five targets shown in the same 'outdated' color, with a legend."
tar_ggplot(node_color = "status", palette = targets_status_colors())
```

## Build it, then plot again

```{r}
#| label: build
tar_make(reporter = "silent")
```

```{r}
#| label: status-after
#| fig-alt: "The same pipeline after tar_make(), all five targets now shown in the 'uptodate' color."
tar_ggplot(node_color = "status", palette = targets_status_colors())
```

Every target is `uptodate` now. Change `fit_model()`'s body (not `raw_data`'s or `clean_data`'s definitions) and only `model` and what depends on it go back to `outdated` - `raw_data` and `clean_data` don't depend on `fit_model()`, so they stay `uptodate`. Without rerunning anything, `tar_ggplot()` shows you exactly what `tar_make()` would rebuild:

```{r}
#| label: edit
tar_script({
  fit_model <- function(data) stats::lm(y ~ x, data = data, weights = NULL)

  list(
    tar_target(raw_data, data.frame(x = 1:20, y = 1:20 * 2 + stats::rnorm(20))),
    tar_target(clean_data, raw_data[stats::complete.cases(raw_data), ]),
    tar_target(model, fit_model(clean_data)),
    tar_target(
      summary,
      data.frame(
        term = names(stats::coef(model)),
        estimate = unname(stats::coef(model))
      )
    ),
    tar_target(
      report,
      paste(utils::capture.output(print(summary)), collapse = "\n")
    )
  )
})
```

```{r}
#| label: status-outdated
#| fig-alt: "The pipeline after editing fit_model()'s body: model and everything downstream of it (summary, report) are outdated again; raw_data and clean_data, which don't depend on fit_model(), stay uptodate."
tar_ggplot(node_color = "status", palette = targets_status_colors())
```

## Filtering

`tar_ggplot()`'s `...` arguments pass straight to [`targets::tar_network()`](https://docs.ropensci.org/targets/reference/tar_network.html), so it filters exactly like `tar_visnetwork()`: `names`/`allow`/`exclude` take [tidyselect](https://tidyselect.r-lib.org/) helpers. `allow` keeps exactly the named targets; `names` keeps them *and* everything upstream they depend on (useful for "show me how target X gets built", not just "show me X"):

```{r}
#| label: filter-allow
#| fig-alt: "Just the model and summary targets, with no other nodes."
tar_ggplot(allow = tidyselect::any_of(c("model", "summary")))
```

```{r}
#| label: filter-names
#| fig-alt: "The model and summary targets plus everything upstream that they depend on (raw_data, clean_data), but not report, which is downstream."
tar_ggplot(names = tidyselect::any_of(c("model", "summary")))
```

```{r}
#| label: filter-exclude
#| fig-alt: "The pipeline with the report target excluded."
tar_ggplot(exclude = tidyselect::starts_with("report"))
```

`targets_only = FALSE` (unlike `tar_ggplot()`'s own default of `TRUE`) also shows imported functions and objects, the way `tar_visnetwork(targets_only = FALSE)` does - useful for seeing exactly what a target depends on, at the cost of a busier plot. Nodes are drawn by their type, as in `tar_visnetwork()`: a regular target is a circle, a dynamic-branching one a square, an imported function an up triangle and an imported object a down triangle, with a legend when more than one shape is drawn.

```{r}
#| label: imports
#| fig-alt: "The pipeline with its imported functions as triangles among the target circles, and a legend of the shapes."
tar_ggplot(targets_only = FALSE)
```

## Customizing the style

Every visual detail is a `style_metro()` argument - bigger nodes, wider arcs, thicker edges:

```{r}
#| label: custom-style
#| fig-alt: "The pipeline drawn larger: bigger nodes, wider bends, thicker edges."
tar_ggplot(
  style = style_metro(
    node_radius = 9,
    arc_radius = 20,
    edge_stroke_width = 3,
    scale = 14
  )
)
```

## Plot size

A plot has a fixed physical size: one data unit is one pixel at 96 dpi. Nodes, lines and text therefore look the same in every pipeline, and a bigger pipeline just gives a bigger plot. `dag_size()` returns that size in inches, legend included. `ggsave_dag()` saves at that size, matching dagviz's own output pixel-for-pixel:

```{r}
#| label: save
p <- tar_ggplot()
dag_size(p)
ggsave_dag(tempfile(fileext = ".png"), p)
```

A large pipeline can be too big for the RStudio Plots pane, which clips it. `zoom` scales nodes, lines and text together. `fixed_size = FALSE` instead stretches the plot to fill the device, like an ordinary ggplot. Line widths and text then no longer stay in proportion to the nodes.

```{r}
#| label: zoom
#| fig-alt: "The same pipeline at half size: smaller nodes, thinner lines and smaller text, all in the same proportions."
tar_ggplot(zoom = 0.5)
```

## Plotting a pipeline in another folder

`tar_ggplot()`'s `script`/`store` arguments locate a pipeline's files, but `targets::tar_network()` (which it wraps) still runs `_targets.R` from the current working directory - and most real pipelines use relative paths, like `tar_source("R")`, that only resolve correctly from the project's own root. The reliable way to plot a pipeline living elsewhere is `withr::with_dir()`:

```{r}
#| label: other-folder
#| fig-alt: "The same five-target pipeline, plotted via withr::with_dir() from outside its own project folder."
# knitr resets the working directory to this vignette's own project folder
# before every chunk, so switch elsewhere just within this one chunk to
# demonstrate the pattern.
setwd(dirname(proj_dir))
getwd() # not the pipeline's own folder
withr::with_dir(proj_dir, tar_ggplot())
```
